proposal: The Mandate recommends that HUD restart the 2019 proposed rule that would prohibit noncitizens, including all mixed-status families, from living in federally assisted housing, and align with DHS public-charge reforms. It states that local welfare organizations, not the federal government, should house noncitizens.
remaining: HUD must review comments, publish a final rule, and set an effective date.
Existing mixed-status households would then have 90 days after the effective date to submit proof of eligible status under the proposal.
The proposal keeps a limited deferral for some long-assisted families, which is narrower than a complete bar.

status_summary: HUD published a new proposed rule on 2026-02-20 (91 FR 8151) that would require immigration or citizenship verification for every household member regardless of age, limit proration of assistance for mixed-status families to the period while verification is pending, and remove the option to decline to claim eligible status. Statutory preservation assistance would remain for families assisted as of HUD's 1995-06-19 reference date, so the proposal does not bar every mixed-status family outright. Comments closed 2026-04-21 and no HUD final rule was found in the Federal Register through 2026-10-13. Separately, a 2025-11-26 HUD notice states that HUD reads PRWORA's federal-public-benefit definition to cover several HUD grant programs and says verification guidance will follow, and HUD's 2026-06-22 notice sought renewal of the existing noncitizen-restriction information collection. DHS published a final public charge rule on 2026-07-20 (effective 2026-09-18) that rescinds the 2022 rule's provisions, a related alignment step that does not change HUD eligibility rules.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14218 (Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Open Borders) is signed; HUD's 2026 proposal cites it as a basis.
HUD publishes a notice interpreting 'federal public benefit' under PRWORA to cover a range of HUD grant and housing programs, with immigration-verification guidance to follow.
HUD posts a pre-publication copy of the proposed rule 'Housing and Community Development Act of 1980: Verification of Eligible Status'.
Proposed rule published at 91 FR 8151: universal status verification, temporary-only proration, end of the 'do not contend' option; 60-day comment period.
Comment period closes. Housing and immigrant-advocacy groups filed opposing comments; no final rule or lawsuit found afterward.

HUD publishes a 60-day notice (91 FR 37121) to extend approval of the existing information collection on the restriction on assistance to noncitizens and the consent form HUD-9886-A, citing section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980; comments were due 2026-08-21, and the notice does not refer to the pending proposed rule.

DHS publishes a final rule on the public charge ground of inadmissibility (91 FR 45324, effective 2026-09-18) that rescinds the 2022 rule's public charge provisions and returns to case-by-case totality-of-the-circumstances assessment, in which receipt of means-tested public benefits may be considered; DHS's impact analysis discusses effects on mixed-status households. This is the DHS counterpart the Mandate asks HUD to align with, but it does not itself change HUD eligibility rules.

title: Bar noncitizens, including mixed-status families, from federally assisted housing
uncertainties: Estimates of affected households (about 80,000 people per an advocacy group's 2025 analysis) are from advocacy sources, not HUD; HUD's own estimates are in the Federal Register text. A Federal Register API query for HUD documents on the proposed rule's title after 2026-04-01 returned none, and a query for HUD documents on noncitizens after 2026-04-22 returned only the 2026-06-22 information collection notice and a 2026-09-30 Privacy Act notice for a HUD data system (which lists citizenship fields and does not describe a new verification process). One general web search (2026-10-13) found only commentary and comment letters from the proposal period; no final rule, OMB review notice, lawsuit or congressional action was found, but a lawsuit would not necessarily appear in those results. The DHS public charge final rule was read only in its first part (the housing assistance section was cut off), so how it treats HUD programs was not verified. Whether a final rule that ends proration fits Section 214 is a legal question not resolved (inference from the statute as described in HUD's proposal).
